title: Selling Attention: Display, Native and Retail-Media Advertising
basis: Reconstructed on 2026-11-12 from the published index.md (paragraph for paragraph, in its own order) and spec.md (accepted 2026-10-21), which it replaces. Intent outcome, acceptance criteria AC-1 to AC-3, the thesis and the role are copied unchanged from the advertising-platforms entry in journal-spec.json; the conclusion realises Part VI's closing (synthesis, so-what, callback, takeaway) from the same file, and the hand-off uses Part VII's part-level transition_in (re-read at the end of the pass, when Part VII had reached full detail). Units added or split by this conversion: introduction p02/p03 (split) and roadmap p04, concepts p12/p13 (split), one lead-in paragraph each for Trade-offs (p40) and Vertical Differences (p42), and a conclusion widened from one paragraph to three (p52 to p54).

know: Advertising as three businesses (display and native, sponsored listings, retail media), the components of a marketplace ad stack and who owns each.
The header-bidding timeout trade-off and page-speed rules for ad slots; why sponsored listings belong inside ranking and the regulatory floor for paid ranking (Omnibus, P2B, DSA Art. 26).
Consent architecture (TCF, certified CMPs, the EDPB consent-or-pay opinion) and a first-party audience service with consent checks, exclusions, minimum sizes and controlled activation.
believe: Consent and latency set the ceiling on display revenue, so changes to them are revenue changes and match-rate changes that need experiments and guardrails.
First-party intent data is the marketplace's advantage and its main liability, and data held in a neutral role stays out of advertising.
can_do: Set an ad-change rule with contacts per session as the guardrail and run the experiment that tests it.
Design an audience service whose segments are consented, purpose-bound and approved by the data-protection officer.
Put every paid position, whoever sells it, under one relevance floor and slot cap and one invoice line.

audience.who: Chief architects, heads of ad tech and data, product and monetization leaders at marketplace groups who own or depend on an advertising unit; data-protection leads who must approve audience products.
already_knows: What an API, a database, an event stream, a search engine, a read model and Kubernetes are; page-speed basics such as largest contentful paint and the 75th percentile.

From earlier chapters: Veldmark (fictional) and its brands Tradeyard, Motorvane, Hearthly, Keybridge and Valuo, the cast (Ingrid Halvorsen, Noor Hassan, Priya Raman, Lucía Ortega, Felix Brandt), the architecture advice forum, Safe Deal, contacts and leads (messaging-and-leads), the relevance floor for top listings and paid-organic blending (ranking), the group product catalog and entitlement effects (products-and-entitlements), guardrail metrics (monetization-models), DSA labels and remunerated-ranking disclosure (marketplace-regulation), and the failure patterns Multiplier Creep, Vanity Liquidity, Billing by Guesswork and Ghost Inventory.
From the part introduction: the test for any paid product (which unit it charges for, what liquidity it spends, how delivery is proved).
does_not_know: The terms this chapter owns: ad stack, first-party audience, sponsored listing.
Ad-industry vocabulary: ad server and line items, SSP, DSP, header bidding and Prebid, PMP deals, native ads, retail media, CMP, TCF and the TC string, ad load, CPM, eCPM, CPC, viewability.
Supply-chain files (ads.txt, app-ads.txt, sellers.json), clean rooms, and the EDPB's consent-or-pay opinion.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given three advertising conflicts, the reader names the component that decides each and the rule it applies.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Your ad unit lengthened the header-bidding timeout and earned about 4% more per thousand page views while listing pages loaded half a second slower; it built an 'in-market' audience for a car maker from search behavior without a consent review; and sellers can buy a fixed-price top listing from the brand and a sponsored campaign from the ad unit for the same rows. Using only this chapter: what decides each, and what rule applies?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Timeouts, slot counts and ad load are set in the ad policy service and ship only behind an experiment with contacts per session as the guardrail; revenue that costs contacts needs a product leadership decision. Audiences come from the first-party audience service, built only from consented, purpose-bound sources approved by the data-protection officer, excluding dealer-side, neutral-role and message data, with a minimum size and off-site activation through a clean room. Both paid products become one product family in the group catalog, decided inside ranking under one relevance floor and slot cap (at most three paid positions in the first ten rows), shown on one invoice line.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading) can predict the chapter's sections.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Advertising as the part's last revenue line and the only one paid for attention rather than matches; the tension between core revenue and page views; the three businesses and the terms the chapter owns; then Veldmark Ads and its three arguments, vocabulary, three stacks under one policy layer, consent, the public record, three 2027 decisions, trade-offs, vertical differences, failure modes, the Chief Architect's view and questions. Evidence: investor sources (Adevinta, eBay, CarGurus, Autotrader, Rightmove), EU law and the EDPB, IAB and Prebid documentation, and the fictional Veldmark.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the chapter, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.

The chapter's last section performs Part VI's closing: it states what the five chapters build in common for every revenue line, says why that matters for Part VII, and returns to the part introduction's test of unit, liquidity spent and proof of delivery.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Does the final section state something about Part VI that no single chapter states, say why it matters for Part VII, and return to the question the part introduction ends on?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A synthesis that every revenue line in the part needs a record both sides can count (lead ID, order and transaction ledger, entitlement ledger, one invoice line for paid positions), delivery events, and a guardrail on the match rate; a so-what that those records need platform support (events, a governed contact definition, guardrails on tests, consent on every event), which Part VII builds; an explicit return to the part introduction's test answered for one paid product.

thesis.question: How do marketplaces run advertising alongside listings without degrading the experience or breaking privacy law?
thesis.claim: Advertising on a listing marketplace is three businesses that should run on three decision paths, display and native through an ad server with header bidding, sponsored listings inside each brand's search and ranking, and retail media through a consented first-party audience service, under one ad policy service, held as configuration by the product organization that owns the page, which sets ad load, labels, exclusions and the floors and caps on paid positions; changes to auction timeouts, slot counts or ad load ship only behind an experiment with contacts per session as the guardrail; fixed-price and auctioned paid positions share one relevance floor and slot cap; and audiences are built only from consented, purpose-bound sources, excluding special-category data, minors and data the group holds in a neutral role.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that advertising is a separate business unit optimized against eCPM, fill rate and revenue per page view, which sets its own timeouts, ad load and sponsored placements on result pages and builds audiences from whatever behavioral data the group holds.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect who accepts this shares the ad server, header bidding, consent integration, audience service and measurement as one group stack but serves sponsored listings inside each brand's ranking, puts all paid positions in one product family in the group catalog, has the data-protection officer approve every audience purpose with exclusions enforced by access control, keeps the campaign, targeting and reporting model group-owned to limit vendor dependency, and shows eCPM and fill rate next to contacts per session and page speed on one dashboard.
thesis.how_why: Veldmark Ads earned €100 million in 2026. Raising the Prebid timeout on Tradeyard Netherlands from 1,000 to 1,500 ms lifted programmatic revenue per thousand page views about 4% but worsened the 75th-percentile largest contentful paint from 2.4 to 2.9 seconds on a site where 46% of sessions start from organic search, and nobody measured contacts; in the July 2027 experiment, 900 ms with server-side bidders and lazy loading lost 1.9% of that revenue and gained about 1% in contacts, which is worth more because contacts drive renewals, VAS purchases and Safe Deal transactions. A car maker's 'electric SUV' segment fell from about 310,000 to about 240,000 users once consent purposes were checked. On Tradeyard Poland a seller could pay twice, on two invoices, for a Top listing and a Sponsored campaign claiming the same rows, the second outside the relevance floor.

supporting_claims.claim: Advertising on a listing marketplace is three businesses with different buyers, auctions, latency budgets and rules (display and native through an ad server with header bidding, sponsored listings inside search and ranking, retail media through placements and first-party audiences), so they run on three decision paths rather than one ad stack.

One ad policy service, held as configuration by the product organization that owns the page, sets ad load, labels, exclusions and the floors and caps on paid positions for all three paths; advertising rents positions under that policy.

Consent and latency set the ceiling on display revenue: the consent record must reach every bid request and audience pipeline server-side, and the auction timeout, slot counts, ad load and the consent dialog are revenue and match-rate parameters that change only behind an experiment with contacts per session as the guardrail.

Sponsored listings are decided inside ranking, and fixed-price and auctioned paid positions are one product family under one relevance floor, one slot cap and one invoice line, with a paid flag carried from campaign to rendering to meet the EU's paid-ranking rules.

A first-party audience is a data product: segments are built only from consented, purpose-bound sources approved by the data-protection officer, exclude special-category data, minors and data held in a neutral or other-purpose role, have minimum sizes, and leave the platform only as identifiers in a clean room, never as exported lists.

At group scale the generic ad stack (ad server, header bidding, consent integration, ads.txt, audience service, measurement) is shared under a group-owned campaign, targeting and reporting model that limits vendor dependency, while sponsored-listing serving stays in each brand's ranking and ad revenue is reported next to contacts and page speed.

role.contribution: Adds the one revenue line paid for attention rather than matches, puts it under the same guardrails and product family as the others, and carries the part's closing into Part VII's platform demands.

additional_patterns.applies_to: scene poses Ingrid's three arguments (timeout against page speed, an unreviewed audience, two products for one position); worked answers each with a decision after the body has built the design
trade-offs, verticals, failure-modes, ca-view, questions: the book's standard judging sections

flow.rationale: The scene comes first because its three arguments are the questions the chapter answers. The concepts follow because every later section uses ad-industry terms (ad server, SSP, header bidding, TC string, first-party audience) that marketplace engineers do not know; the scene glosses header bidding in passing. The architecture then lays out the three decision paths and the policy layer, path by path; consent follows it because its consequences name components the architecture introduced (Prebid Server, the audience service, app backends) and cut across all three paths; placed before the architecture, consent would be a list of rules for systems the reader has not seen. The public record comes right after the vocabulary and before the design, as the evidence that motivates it: advertising is large and cyclical on horizontals, and sponsored listings and audiences are decided in the marketplace's own systems; placed after the design, as first published, it repeated sources the architecture had already cited and separated consent from the worked example that applies it. The worked example can only replay the scene's three arguments once the timeout rule, the audience-service rules and the sponsored-listing design exist. Trade-offs, vertical differences, failure modes, the Chief Architect's view and the questions apply the whole design, so they come last, and the conclusion closes Part VI.

hook.content: A marketplace earns its core revenue when buyers find the right listing quickly; it earns advertising revenue when they look at more pages.

bridge.from_reader_world: Part VI so far: messaging-and-leads turned contacts into leads, monetization-models chose what to charge for, and products-and-entitlements proved that what was sold was delivered, all revenue paid for matches.
bridge.to_topic: Advertising, the part's last revenue line and the only one paid for attention, sold to brands that sell nothing on the marketplace, so the architecture must decide where the balance between pages viewed and matches made is enforced.

thesis_statement.text: Advertising is three businesses (display and native, sponsored listings, retail media) built as three products under one shared policy layer for labels, ad load, consent and data use; consent and latency changes are revenue changes that need experiments and guardrails; first-party intent data is used only through consented, purpose-bound segments that exclude sensitive and neutral-role data.

sections.heading: Setting the Scene at Veldmark: One Ad Unit, Three Arguments
sections.controlling_idea: Veldmark Ads, a €100 million shared unit, faced three arguments in one week of June 2027 (a longer auction against page speed, an unreviewed audience, two products for one position), which pose the chapter's question of which parts of advertising are one platform, which slots and data each may use and who decides conflicts.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the cost of a timeout set without contacts, an audience built without consent review and paid positions sold outside ranking, and poses the questions the body answers.

flow.rationale: The unit and its revenue come first so the reader knows what is at stake; the three arguments follow, each a problem one of the later decisions answers; Ingrid's question closes the section so the reader carries it into the vocabulary and design.

transition_in.carries_over: The three businesses and the conflict between pages viewed and matches made.
transition_in.introduces: Veldmark Ads as the running example.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Veldmark runs one shared advertising unit, Veldmark Ads, which earned €100 million in 2026 on Google Ad Manager with Prebid header bidding (glossed as an auction run before the ad server decides), split across four products with different buyers and different places where they run: the three businesses, with display and native sold two ways, programmatic (through supply-side platforms, glossed, in the open auction or in private deals offered to selected buyers) and direct, and the prose maps the table's rows to the three businesses before the Concepts section defines the remaining terms.

evidence.shows: The four products have different buyers and run in different systems, which is the chapter's first claim.

sections.heading: Concepts: The Vocabulary of the Ad Stack
sections.controlling_idea: Two distinctions, media sold to advertisers versus visibility sold to sellers, and the first-party audience as a data product, shape the chapter, and a short vocabulary of ad-industry terms makes the rest readable.

advances_thesis.how: Separates display from sponsored listings and treats audiences as data products, the basis of two supporting claims.

transition_in.carries_over: Ingrid's question about which parts are one platform.
transition_in.introduces: The distinctions and terms needed to answer it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Display and native ads are a media business sold to advertisers who may have no listings, sponsored listings are a visibility product sold to sellers about their listings, and a first-party audience is a data product that needs purpose limitation, access control and ownership.

evidence.what: The two distinctions and the pointer to data-platform for data products.
evidence.shows: Grounds why sponsored listings belong with visibility products and why audiences need data-product governance.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A table defines the ad-industry terms the chapter uses, most unfamiliar to marketplace engineers, from the ad stack and ad server to header bidding, the data clean room, the TC string, ad load and viewability.

evidence.what: Sixteen definitions: ad stack, ad server, SSP, DSP, header bidding and Prebid, PMP deal, native ad, sponsored listing, retail media, data clean room, first-party audience, CMP with TCF and TC string, ad load, CPM/eCPM/CPC, viewability with the MRC 50%-for-one-second rule.
evidence.source: MRC Viewable Ad Impression Guidelines v2.0 (2015) for viewability
evidence.shows: Gives the reader every term the architecture and consent sections rely on; the three owned terms are marked.

transition_in.introduces: The vocabulary the chapter uses.

sections.heading: Architecture: Three Stacks, One Policy Layer
sections.controlling_idea: Veldmark's reference design keeps the display, sponsored-listing and retail-media decision paths apart, each with its own rules, and puts one policy service over all of them.

advances_thesis.how: Lays out the three paths and the policy layer, path by path, with the rules each path needs.

flow.rationale: The overview and component table come first; then each path in turn, display (with native placements, which share its ad server), sponsored listings, retail media and the audience service, ordered from the most generic to the most marketplace-specific, so each path can be contrasted with the one before.

transition_in.carries_over: The vocabulary's two distinctions: display and native ads are sold to advertisers, sponsored listings to sellers about their listings, and a first-party audience is a data product.
transition_in.introduces: The reference architecture that follows: three decision paths kept apart because buyers and deciding systems differ, under one policy service because they share pages, users and consent.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Veldmark's reference architecture keeps three decision paths apart and puts one policy service, owned by the product organization as configuration, over all of them, with a named owner for each component.

evidence.what: Figure 1: display and native decided by the ad server after header bidding, sponsored listings inside the search stack, retail media using both plus the audience service; one policy service sets ad load, labels, exclusions and floors; measurement reports contacts next to revenue.
evidence.shows: Shows the three paths and the one policy layer at a glance.

evidence.what: Eight components with responsibility and owner: CMP (group privacy), header bidding, ad server, audience service (Veldmark Ads with Data & ML; DPO approves purposes), sponsored listing auction (each brand's search team), campaign and budget service, ad policy service (Group CPO's organization; configuration, not code), measurement and billing.
evidence.shows: Each component has one owner, and the policy and sponsored-listing decisions are owned outside the ad unit.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the three paths and the policy service.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A display impression on a listing page is a short distributed transaction with a hard deadline, from consent through bid requests, the ad server's decision and rendering to impression and viewability reports.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the deadline and the consent string on the display path.

transition_in.introduces: The display path, step by step.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The header-bidding timeout trades bids against page speed, as Prebid's documentation says, and because apps cannot run browser header bidding, server-side bidding through Prebid Server is not optional for a marketplace with much app traffic.

evidence.what: Prebid: late bidders 'will not be included in the auction'; finding the balance 'might require some time and experimentation'; Prebid Server 'required in environments that don't have HTML header sections'; Prebid Mobile works 'in conjunction with Prebid Server'.
evidence.shows: The trade-off is documented by the tool itself, and apps need the server-side path.

evidence.what: Figure 2: one display impression, timeout bounding the bid step, late bids dropped, consent string on every request, lazy-loaded slots below the fold.
evidence.shows: Shows where the timeout and consent string sit in the request.

advances_thesis.how: Makes the timeout a revenue and page-speed parameter.

transition_in.carries_over: A transaction with a hard deadline.
transition_in.introduces: The trade-off that deadline creates and the server-side path.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Five rules keep the auction off the page's critical path: never block listing content, reserve slot dimensions, lazy-load below-the-fold slots, move heavy bidders server-side, and treat the timeout as a product parameter with an owner and an experiment measured on contacts.

advances_thesis.how: Ends in the rule that timeouts are measured on contacts as well as revenue.

transition_in.introduces: The rules that limit its cost to the page.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Supply-chain hygiene is part of the stack: ads.txt, app-ads.txt and sellers.json declare who may sell the inventory and must be kept in step with every SSP contract, per domain, app and brand.

evidence.what: IAB Tech Lab: ads.txt lets a publisher declare authorized sellers, 'making it harder for bad actors to profit from selling counterfeit inventory'.
evidence.shows: These small files are configuration that must track contracts.

advances_thesis.how: Names shared configuration the group stack must manage.

transition_in.introduces: The configuration around the auction.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The ad server is a dependency to manage: Google Ad Manager is a reasonable default but a concentration risk after the April 2025 US antitrust ruling, so line items, targeting keys, creatives and reporting belong in a group-owned model that makes the ad server replaceable in a quarter.

evidence.what: US Department of Justice (2025): a court held Google 'violated antitrust law by monopolizing open-web digital advertising markets'.
evidence.shows: Remedies may change the product, so dependency is a real risk.

advances_thesis.how: Argues for the group-owned campaign model that limits vendor dependency.

transition_in.introduces: The largest vendor dependency in the stack.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Native ads are not a fourth path but placements the display path's ad server fills inside the result list; they must be labeled as advertising under the DSA, and their positions count against the same ad-load budget as the sponsored listings described next, because each is a position not given to the most relevant listing.

evidence.what: DSA Art. 26(1): recipients identify 'in a clear, concise and unambiguous manner and in real time' that the information is an advertisement, on whose behalf and who paid.
evidence.shows: Labels are a legal requirement on every native unit.

advances_thesis.how: Puts native and sponsored positions under one ad-load budget set by the policy layer.

transition_in.carries_over: The display path and its ad server.
transition_in.introduces: Native placements, which the same ad server fills inside the listing grid.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Sponsored listings are the advertising product closest to the core marketplace, and public sources from eBay and OLX show that paid visibility lives inside ranking whatever team sells it.

evidence.what: eBay FY2025 10-K: Promoted Listings 'a first-party advertising offering' producing 'a meaningful amount of our revenue'; advertising revenue US$1,993M against US$79.6B GMV.
evidence.shows: Sponsored listings can be a large business.

evidence.what: OLX Tech Blog (2025): a 'VAS LTR' model balancing relevance and visibility for paid listings, retrained when vector retrieval changed which paid listings were retrieved.
evidence.shows: Paid visibility is a ranking concern in practice.

evidence.what: Figure 3: campaigns and budgets in the ad unit's service; the decision which paid listings appear, where, above a relevance floor, made inside ranking from a read model; billing and attribution consume impression and click events.
evidence.shows: Shows the split between selling and deciding.

advances_thesis.how: Places the sponsored-listing decision inside ranking.

transition_in.carries_over: Native ads, filled by the ad server.
transition_in.introduces: Sponsored listings, which belong to the search stack.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Five design choices keep paid positions inside the marketplace's rules: the auction runs inside ranking from a read model, budgets are paced, invalid traffic is filtered before billing, attribution reports contacts, and sponsored and fixed-price visibility products are one product family.

evidence.what: A campaign with €300 a day should not spend it in the first hour of a Sunday peak; overspend of a few percent is credited.
evidence.shows: Shows pacing tolerating the staleness of a read model.

advances_thesis.how: Argues for one product family and the auction inside ranking.

transition_in.introduces: The design choices that follow from it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: EU law sets a clear floor for paid ranking (undisclosed paid ranking is blacklisted for consumers, and business users must be told how payment affects ranking), so a sponsored listing needs a machine-readable paid flag from campaign to rendering.

evidence.what: Directive (EU) 2019/2161, UCPD Annex I point 11a: search results without clearly disclosing paid advertisement or payment for higher ranking; Regulation (EU) 2019/1150 Art. 5: describe the possibility to influence ranking against remuneration and its effects.
evidence.shows: Both laws require the paid flag and a product description for sellers.

advances_thesis.how: Adds the paid flag to the sponsored-listing design.

transition_in.carries_over: The design choices for sponsored listings.
transition_in.introduces: The legal floor they must meet.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Retail media sells brands placements, audiences and measurement against outcomes the marketplace can see, as CarGurus, Autotrader and Rightmove show in their filings.

evidence.what: CarGurus FY2025 10-K: 'Audience Targeting' retargeting off site by 'geography, search history, CarGurus website activity', plus manufacturer and 'non-endemic programmatic advertisers'.
evidence.shows: The audience product exists in automotive marketplaces.

evidence.what: Rightmove: about 10 million consumers subscribed to its marketing CRM, placed after the CarGurus audience product; Autotrader FY26: Manufacturer & Agency revenue £15.2M, up 14%, expected to grow in FY27, small next to £585.3M Autotrader revenue but reported on its own and growing.
evidence.shows: Rightmove's figure shows that a vertical leader holds a large first-party audience it reaches without any third party, the raw material of audience products; Autotrader's shows that retail media is a real, separately reported revenue line.

advances_thesis.how: Shows retail media as a distinct business built on audiences.

transition_in.introduces: The third path: retail media.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The first-party audience service concentrates the privacy risk, so Veldmark's five rules make segments reviewed data, check consent at build and activation, exclude special-category, minors' and neutral-role data at the source, never export raw data, and protect sellers' interests.

evidence.what: DSA Art. 26(3): no ads 'based on profiling … using special categories of personal data'; Art. 28(2): no profiling-based ads to recipients known 'with reasonable certainty' to be minors.
evidence.shows: The exclusions are legal floors, enforced at the source category.

evidence.what: A car maker's audience built from Motorvane searches is, to a dealer, Motorvane selling its dealers' buyers to a competitor; Keybridge's agency CRM data is out of scope by policy and access control.
evidence.shows: Seller interests and neutral-role data are architectural constraints, not only legal ones.

advances_thesis.how: States the audience-service rules.

transition_in.introduces: Where that concentrates privacy risk and the rules that contain it.

sections.heading: Consent: The Signal That Sets the Revenue
sections.controlling_idea: Consent determines how much inventory can be sold with personalized targeting, so the consent record, the consent dialog and the fallback for users who decline are architecture decisions with revenue and legal consequences.

advances_thesis.how: Shows consent as the signal that sets display revenue and gates audiences.

flow.rationale: The legal and industry frame comes first, then three consequences from the most technical (where the record lives) to the most strategic (what decliners see), and finally the dependency on third-party identifiers that the contextual fallback reduces.

transition_in.carries_over: The three paths, each of which carries or checks consent.
transition_in.introduces: Consent as the signal they all depend on.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: All three paths depend on consent: EU law requires consent to read or store device identifiers, the industry encodes it through IAB Europe's TCF (v2.3, with a 28 February 2026 adoption deadline), and Google requires a certified TCF-integrated CMP for personalized ads in the EEA and UK since 16 January 2024.

evidence.what: IAB Europe TCF versions v1.1 (2018) to v2.3 (April 2025); 'TCF participants have until 28 February 2026 to adopt TCF v2.3'; Disclosed Vendors segment mandatory.
evidence.shows: The consent string has a versioned format the stack must keep up with.

evidence.what: Google Ad Manager Help: 'a certified CMP integrated with the TCF', in force since 16 January 2024; traffic without it may still receive non-personalized or limited ads.
evidence.shows: Without a certified CMP, personalized demand disappears.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The first of three architectural consequences is that consent is per user, device, purpose and vendor and it changes, so the CMP's record must be available server-side to Prebid Server, the audience service and app backends, and withdrawals must propagate within a stated time.

advances_thesis.how: Requires the consent record on every bid request and audience build.

transition_in.introduces: Three architectural consequences, and the first: where the consent record lives.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The consent dialog is a revenue component and the most regulator-visible design decision in the stack, so changes to it belong under experimentation with legal review, not under a growth team's control.

advances_thesis.how: Treats the dialog as a governed revenue parameter.

transition_in.introduces: The second consequence: the dialog that creates it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Consent or pay is not a safe default after the EDPB's 2024 opinion, so the more robust design is consent or contextual, which a listing marketplace does unusually well because the page states the intent.

evidence.what: EDPB Opinion 08/2024 (17 April 2024): 'in most cases, it will not be possible for them to comply with the requirements for valid consent'; consider a free alternative 'without behavioural advertising'.
evidence.shows: A binary pay-or-track choice is legally fragile.

evidence.what: No classifieds marketplace was on the Commission's list of designated very large online platforms when checked in October 2026.
evidence.shows: The opinion was addressed to large online platforms, so it does not bind Veldmark directly; the prose states this link, and the opinion still sets the direction for everyone.

evidence.what: Figure 4: consent or contextual, decliners see ads targeted by category, location and price band.
evidence.shows: Shows the fallback path.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the design for users who decline.

transition_in.introduces: The third consequence: what users who decline see.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Contextual targeting also keeps a marketplace's dependence on third-party identifiers low, which matters because browser identity plans keep changing, as Google's 2025 reversal on third-party cookies and Privacy Sandbox showed.

evidence.what: Google (October 2025): Chrome would 'maintain our current approach to offering users third-party cookie choice' and retire Topics and Protected Audience, citing 'low levels of adoption'.
evidence.shows: Identity plumbing outside the marketplace's control changes without notice.

advances_thesis.how: Supports first-party identity as part of limiting dependency.

transition_in.carries_over: Contextual targeting, which needs no third-party identifier.
transition_in.introduces: Why reducing that dependency matters.

sections.heading: In Practice: What the Public Record Shows
sections.controlling_idea: Public filings show advertising is large on horizontals, cyclical, built on SSPs as critical suppliers and, for sponsored listings and audiences, decided in the marketplace's own systems.

advances_thesis.how: Grounds the three businesses and the shared-stack argument in documented company facts.

transition_in.carries_over: The three paths and the consent rules, whose real-company evidence was cited along the way.
transition_in.introduces: The public record collected in one place, and the one lesson it adds: display revenue is cyclical.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The three paths and the consent rules rest on what marketplaces have published; they publish advertising revenue more readily than architecture, but their figures, most of them cited in the paths above and collected here in one place, show how large and cyclical the business is and where its decisions run.

evidence.what: Seven rows: Adevinta 2023 advertising €312M of €1,826M (about 17%), €204M of €744M (about 27%) in European Markets, France down 7%; SSPs as key suppliers and revenue 'recognised as the ads are displayed'; first-party advertising in the convergence plan; eBay US$1,993M; CarGurus audience targeting; Autotrader £15.2M (+14%) next to £585.3M revenue; OLX VAS LTR.
evidence.shows: Each row's last column states what it shows: size, fragility, dependencies, and that paid visibility is a ranking concern.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Display advertising follows the advertising market, not the marketplace's liquidity, so a group should never plan platform investments on display revenue growing with audience.

evidence.what: Adevinta European Markets earned more than a quarter of revenue from advertising while France reported a 7% decline driven by agencies and programmatic demand; Adevinta has been private since 2024.
evidence.shows: Display revenue moves with the ad market, not with matches.

transition_in.introduces: The lesson they support.

sections.heading: Veldmark Worked Example: Three Decisions in 2027
sections.controlling_idea: In July 2027 the architecture advice forum answered the scene's three arguments with three decisions: a timeout set with contacts as the guardrail, audiences rebuilt from approved building blocks, and one product family of paid positions.

advances_thesis.how: Applies the guardrail rule, the audience rules and the one-product-family rule to the scene's cases, with numbers.

flow.rationale: The decisions follow the order of the scene's arguments, so each answer meets its problem in the same position; within each decision, the evidence comes before the rule adopted.

transition_in.carries_over: The scene's three arguments, the design and consent rules that answer them, and the public record's caution that display revenue follows the ad market.
transition_in.introduces: The decisions the forum took.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: With the record's caution about display revenue in mind, the architecture advice forum took three decisions in July 2027, one for each of the scene's three arguments, each with a decision record.

evidence.what: Three decisions in July 2027, each recorded.
evidence.shows: Signals that the scene's three arguments are answered in order.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Priya Raman's team tested the timeout in a four-week user-randomized experiment on Tradeyard Netherlands with three arms, and the arm at 900 ms with server-side bidders and lazy loading was fastest and produced the most contacts.

evidence.what: Arms 1,500 ms / 900 ms / 900 ms server-side and lazy-load: programmatic revenue per 1,000 page views 100 / 96.8 / 98.1; LCP p75 2.9 / 2.5 / 2.3 s; search-to-contact rate 100 / 100.5 / 100.9; contacts per 1,000 sessions 100 / 100.6 / 101.0.
evidence.shows: Shows that shorter, server-side auctions trade a small revenue loss for faster pages and more contacts.

transition_in.introduces: Decision 1: the experiment on the auction timeout.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The forum adopted the third arm because about 1% more contacts is worth more than 1.9% of programmatic revenue, and made a rule that every change to ad timeouts, slot counts or ad load ships behind an experiment with contacts per session as the guardrail, with revenue that costs contacts decided by the CPO.

evidence.what: Contacts drive renewals, VAS purchases and Safe Deal transactions; Noor Hassan decides revenue that requires fewer contacts.
evidence.shows: Explains why the contact gain outweighs the revenue loss.

evidence.what: Figure 5: a balance scale with the faster page and more contacts outweighing slightly more ad revenue; a contacts gate for ad changes.
evidence.shows: Shows the guardrail rule.

advances_thesis.how: States the guardrail rule.

transition_in.introduces: The decision and the general rule drawn from them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The car maker's electric-SUV audience was rebuilt from approved building blocks (Motorvane searches and saved searches in 30 days, consented users only, no dealer, Keybridge, Valuo or contact data, at least 1,000 users, off site only through a clean room), and the consent check cut it from about 310,000 to about 240,000 users, a 23% difference the original had ignored.

evidence.what: Segment of about 310,000 users in Germany falling to about 240,000 after the consent check; minimum 1,000 users per activation; private deals and on-site activation; off site only via clean room with aggregate reporting.
evidence.shows: Shows the audience-service rules applied, and what an unchecked segment had silently included.

evidence.what: Figure 6: an audience tower built from approved blocks only, excluded data outside, shrunk by a consent filter, off-site use only through a clean room.
evidence.shows: Shows the rules as one picture.

advances_thesis.how: Applies the audience rules with numbers.

transition_in.introduces: Decision 2: the audience rebuilt.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The forum accepted Felix Brandt's condition that car makers' retail-media placements stay off Motorvane dealer listing detail pages, because dealers paying €238 million a year in subscriptions matter more than a €14 million retail-media line.

evidence.what: Motorvane dealer subscriptions €238M a year against €14M of retail media; placements only on search, editorial and model pages; dealers see which placements ran next to their stock.
evidence.shows: Seller trust outweighs the advertising revenue at stake.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the policy layer enforcing a commercial exclusion.

transition_in.introduces: A second condition on the same retail-media deal: where its placements may appear.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Decision 3 took effect later, from Q1 2028: Top listing and Sponsored on Tradeyard Poland became one product family, two pricing modes for one slot type read by ranking from one read model under the relevance floor, with at most three paid positions in the first ten rows and one invoice line per seller per period.

evidence.what: Sponsored-listing revenue on Tradeyard Poland fell about 6% in the first months of 2028, after the floor, while contacts per paid position rose; Veldmark Ads keeps the auction, budgets and self-serve tool; the brand keeps the product description and slot rules.
evidence.shows: One floor and cap cost some revenue and raised the value of each paid position, the pattern ranking reports for top listings.

advances_thesis.how: Applies one product family, one floor, one cap and one invoice line.

transition_in.introduces: Decision 3: one family of paid positions, signposted as taking effect later, from Q1 2028.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.controlling_idea: Most ad-stack choices have two defensible options that depend on scale, privacy posture and the matching business, and the general rule is to own the decisions that use the marketplace's listings and audiences and rent the plumbing for generic display.

advances_thesis.how: Separates what a marketplace should own from what it should rent.

transition_in.carries_over: The design and its three applications.
transition_in.introduces: The choices behind it, with the conditions for each option.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: For seven recurring ad-stack choices, a table gives two options and the conditions under which each is right.

evidence.what: Ad server, header bidding, sponsored-listings owner, audience activation, users who decline consent, ad load, sales: option A, option B, when each is right.
evidence.shows: Each option is right under named conditions; contextual for decliners and low, contact-guarded ad load are right almost always for marketplaces.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An in-house display ad server is rarely justified because demand sits in the programmatic ecosystem, but sponsored listings and retail media are decided in the marketplace's own systems anyway, so a marketplace should own the decisions that use its listings and audiences and rent the plumbing for generic display.

transition_in.introduces: The rule that sums them up.

sections.heading: Vertical Differences
sections.controlling_idea: Advertising's revenue share, buyers, sensitive data and main conflict differ by vertical, and real estate shows how a vertical's sensitive data shapes the audience rules.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the audience exclusions and the three businesses varying by vertical.

transition_in.introduces: How the same choices differ by vertical.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Advertising differs by vertical in revenue share, buyers, sensitive data and main conflict.

evidence.what: General classifieds, real estate, automotive, jobs, recommerce across share of revenue from ads, main buyers, sponsored listings, sensitive data risk and main conflict.
evidence.shows: Each vertical has its own sensitive data and its own conflict between advertising and sellers or users.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In real estate a property search reveals a household's budget and life events, so Hearthly's mortgage and insurance advertisers buy contextual placements and consented search audiences, and never segments derived from Valuo valuation requests, which were collected for another purpose.

evidence.what: The Hearthly rule: contextual placements by price band and region, audiences only from consented search behavior, no Valuo-derived segments.
evidence.shows: Purpose limitation applied to a vertical's most sensitive data.

advances_thesis.how: Applies the other-purpose exclusion.

transition_in.introduces: The real-estate case at Veldmark.

sections.heading: Failure Modes
sections.controlling_idea: Advertising fails in recognizable ways when it escapes ranking, measures only revenue, stops consent at the browser, builds or exports audiences without controls, competes with sellers, runs unrestricted scripts, lets seller files go stale or keeps gone listings alive.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the cost of ignoring each supporting claim.

transition_in.carries_over: What the right design looks like across verticals.
transition_in.introduces: What goes wrong without it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Without the design, advertising fails in nine ways, from sponsored units inserted after ranking (Multiplier Creep by a second door) to ads on gone listings, where the lead-in says the last item carries the book's Ghost Inventory pattern (sold or removed listings that stay visible) into advertising.

sections.heading: The Chief Architect's View
sections.controlling_idea: At group scale the Chief Architect decides five things about advertising: what is shared, who owns the page, what data advertising may use, how dependent to be, and how to measure.

advances_thesis.how: Turns the design into group-level decisions.

flow.rationale: One paragraph per question, from the structural (what is shared, who owns the page) to the operational (data, dependency, measurement), so the last question returns to the contacts the chapter measures against.

transition_in.introduces: The questions a Chief Architect owns to prevent them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: At group scale, preventing these failures raises five questions for the Chief Architect's agenda.

The ad server, header bidding, CMP integration, ads.txt management, audience service and measurement are generic and belong to one group stack, while sponsored-listing serving belongs inside each brand's ranking and paid positions in the group product catalog.

advances_thesis.how: States what is shared and what is not.

transition_in.introduces: The first: what is shared.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A listing page has one owner, the brand's product team, and advertising rents positions on it under a policy the product organization sets as configuration in the ad policy service.

advances_thesis.how: Places the policy layer with the product organization.

transition_in.introduces: The second question: who owns the page.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The audience service is a data product with DPO-approved purposes and hard exclusions (special categories, minors, Keybridge's neutral-role data, Valuo's other-purpose data), and every segment has an owner, a definition, a size and an activation log.

advances_thesis.how: Restates the audience rules as a group responsibility.

transition_in.introduces: The third question: what data advertising may use.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A display business on one vendor's ad server and one browser's identity choices has two dependencies it does not control, so the campaign, targeting and reporting model stays group-owned, identity stays first-party and the exit plan is reviewed when the landscape changes.

advances_thesis.how: Limits vendor dependency.

transition_in.introduces: The fourth question: how dependent to be.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The group dashboard shows advertising's revenue, eCPM, fill rate and viewability next to contacts per session, search-to-contact rate and page speed, so measurement puts back the matches advertising does not depend on.

advances_thesis.how: Puts contacts next to ad revenue.

transition_in.introduces: The fifth question: how to measure.

sections.heading: Questions to Ask
sections.controlling_idea: Ten questions let an architect test a marketplace's advertising against the chapter: paid positions under one floor, the timeout, consent reach, decliners, audience approval, exclusions, seller visibility, vendor exit, supply-chain files and labels.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the reader a working audit drawn from every section.

transition_in.introduces: Detailed questions that test whether they are answered.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Ten questions test the Chief Architect's five answers: whether a marketplace's paid positions, timeouts, consent, audiences, exclusions, seller visibility, vendor dependency, seller files and labels meet the chapter's design.

conclusion.heading: From Revenue to the Platform Underneath
conclusion.synthesis: The five chapters of Part VI give every revenue line three things: a record both sides can count (the lead ID, the order and transaction ledger, the entitlement ledger, and one invoice line for all paid positions), delivery events that prove the record, and a guardrail on what the line costs in contacts. Money is one pipeline because those records and guardrails are shared, not because one team sells everything.
conclusion.so_what: Those records and guardrails are platform demands: the ad stack needs a consent signal on every event, a read model of paid positions inside ranking and measurement joining impressions to contacts, and the earlier chapters need leads and paid effects as events, one governed contact definition and guardrails on pricing tests; these are platform problems, which Part VII builds the shared platform to solve.

callback.to: The Part VI introduction's closing test (for any paid product, which unit it charges for, what liquidity it spends and how you would prove it was delivered).
callback.how: The reader can now answer the test for a Sponsored campaign on Tradeyard Poland from the chapter's design: a position priced per click; the organic listings it pushes down, within the relevance floor and three paid positions in the first ten rows; impression and click events from ranking proving delivery on one invoice line.

takeaway.content: Review every revenue change for its cost in contacts, with its record, delivery evidence and guardrail named before launch; Part VII begins with event-driven-listings, the event backbone these records ride on.

hand_off.carries_over: The ad stack needed a consent signal on every event, a read model of paid positions inside ranking and measurement that joins impressions to contacts, and Part VI as a whole assumed events for leads and paid effects, contact counts and pricing tests without building them.
hand_off.introduces: The distributed system beneath every stage: events, copies, the public web, data, experimentation, ML, tenancy and reliability, starting with the event backbone in event-driven-listings.

transition_in.carries_over: The whole chapter, from Veldmark Ads' three arguments to the review questions, and the four Part VI chapters before it.
transition_in.introduces: The answer to the chapter's question, then what Part VI's five chapters share.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Ingrid's question is answered: the ad stack and one policy layer are shared, the policy service and DPO-approved audience blocks set which slots and data each business may use, and the forum settles conflicts, with the CPO deciding revenue that costs contacts.

advances_thesis.how: Answers the chapter's question from the scene with the design.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: That answer is one instance of what the part builds: Part VI's five chapters give every revenue line a record both sides can count, delivery events that prove it and a guardrail on what it costs in contacts, so money is one pipeline because its records and guardrails are shared, not because one team sells everything.

evidence.what: The lead ID (messaging-and-leads), the order and transaction ledger (transactions-and-payments), the entitlement ledger (products-and-entitlements) and one invoice line for paid positions (this chapter).
evidence.shows: Each chapter builds one such record; none states that they share a shape.

advances_thesis.how: Places the chapter's one invoice line and shared stack within the part's common records.

transition_in.carries_over: The chapter's answer to Ingrid's question.
transition_in.introduces: The part's synthesis, of which that answer is one instance.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The part introduction's test can now be answered for a Sponsored campaign on Tradeyard Poland: it charges per click for a position, spends the organic listings it pushes down within the relevance floor and slot cap, and is proved delivered by impression and click events on the seller's one invoice line.

evidence.what: Tradeyard Poland Sponsored (cost per click) under the relevance floor and at most three paid positions in the first ten rows, from Q1 2028; impression and click events consumed by billing.
evidence.shows: The part's three-part test is answered by this chapter's design.

advances_thesis.how: Answers the test with the one-product-family design.

transition_in.carries_over: Records, delivery events and guardrails shared across the part.
transition_in.introduces: The part introduction's test applied to one paid product of this chapter.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: These records depend on systems beneath every brand (for the ad stack: consent on every event, a read model of paid positions, measurement joining impressions to contacts; for the earlier chapters: leads and paid effects as events, a governed contact definition, guardrails on tests); because those are platform problems, every revenue change should be reviewed for its cost in contacts, and Part VII turns to that distributed platform, starting with the event backbone.

advances_thesis.how: Turns the consent and guardrail demands into the hand-off.

transition_in.carries_over: A test answered from shared records.
transition_in.introduces: What those records demand of the platform, and the hand-off to Part VII.
